                            BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS

                                 PETITION FOR ADOPTION OF A RULE
                                    Measurement and Reporting of Resource Consumption
                                             by Large Computational Loads

                                          Proposed new 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.___
                        Filed pursuant to Tex. Gov't Code § 2001.021 and 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 22.281


                                          Petitioner: Green Recursive Utility Service LLC
                                            Nicholas Wray Cordova, Principal
                                      205 East 3rd Street, Weatherford, Texas 76086
                         Texas SOS 806584578 · SAM UEI JGT4J9QKGCQ3 · PUCT Control No. 59976
                                management@greenrecursiveutilityservice.org · 817-404-6379




   Document Control

    Document                           Petition for adoption of a rule, filed under Tex. Gov't Code § 2001.021 and 16 Tex. Admin.
                                       Code § 22.281

    Proposed rule                      New 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.___, Measurement and Reporting of Resource
                                       Consumption by Large Computational Loads. Designation subject to assignment by the
                                       Commission; placement proposed in Chapter 25, Subchapter I, adjacent to § 25.194.

    Source                             GRUS-STD-60084 v2.0, The Measurement Standard for Large Computational Loads, filed
                                       of record in Project No. 60084. This petition converts that document to rulemaking form.
                                       No substantive position has been removed, condensed, or withdrawn.

    Markup convention                  Per § 22.281(a)(1), proposed additions are indicated by underlining. The section
                                       proposed is new in its entirety; no existing rule text is amended or deleted, so no
                                       strikethrough appears. Proposed rule text appears in bordered blocks labeled
                                       PROPOSED RULE TEXT. Material outside those blocks is basis and justification and is
                                       not proposed for adoption.

    Severability                       Each subsection is drafted to stand independently. The Commission may adopt any
                                       subsection, or any combination, without adopting the remainder. Subsection (n) so
                                       provides.

    Incorporation                      Annexes A through J and Exhibits 1 through 5 are incorporated by reference at
                                       subsection (m) and are reproduced in full at the end of this petition, exactly as filed.

    Neutrality                         The measurement specifications use only published, vendor-neutral figures and off-the-
                                       shelf instrumentation. No proprietary mechanism is required to comply. No vendor,
                                       utility, or verifier holds any exclusive position under the proposed rule. Petitioner seeks
                                       no exclusive role.

    License                            Petitioner places the proposed rule text and the incorporated technical appendix in the
                                       public domain for regulatory use. Adoption requires no license from, and confers no
                                       exclusive right upon, Petitioner.



   Contents

    Part I               Purpose and Statutory Frame

    Part II              Why Self-Reporting Is Insufficient as a Matter of Record




GRUS · Petition for Adoption of a Rule · 16 TAC § 25.___ · PUC Project No. 60084                                              Page 1 of 33
     Part III             The Independence-of-Judgment Standard Already in Texas Law
    Part IV              The Classification Framework — Engineering Basis
                         IV.A Hardware sourcing · IV.B Density classes and the air-cooling limit · IV.C The deterministic
                         heat-and-water chain · IV.D Axis 1, workload classes · IV.E Axis 2, cooling classes · IV.F The
                         two-axis matrix · IV.G Uniformity and the socialization gap
    Part V               Proposed Rule Text, Subsections (a) through (n), with Basis
    Part VI              Why Each Element Belongs Inside the Measurement

    Part VII             Request and Signature
                         Statutory and Regulatory References
    Annexes              A through J, incorporated by reference at subsection (m)
    Exhibits             1 through 5, incorporated by reference at subsection (m)


   How to Read This Petition

   Parts I through III state the purpose, the statutory frame, and the reason self-reporting cannot satisfy the
   audit the State has already ordered. Part IV supplies the engineering basis for the classification framework
   — the two axes against which any facility is read — stated entirely from published, vendor-neutral figures
   so that it can be applied by any reviewer without access to proprietary data.

   Part V is the proposed rule. Each subsection appears in a bordered block as proposed rule text, followed by
   its basis in ordinary type. The bordered blocks, taken together and in order, are the complete proposed text
   of 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.___ and satisfy the requirement of § 22.281(a)(1). Nothing outside a bordered
   block is proposed for adoption.

   Part VI explains why each subsection is part of the measurement rather than an addition to it. Part VII is
   the request. The Technical Annexes are incorporated by reference at subsection (m) and are not
   appendices of convenience. Annex I in particular states every formula used anywhere in this petition,
   together with the worked arithmetic, so that any reviewing engineer can reproduce or refute each number
   without contacting Petitioner.



                               PART I — PURPOSE AND STATUTORY FRAME

   Procedural posture. This petition requests adoption of a rule of general applicability under Tex. Gov't
   Code § 2001.021 and the Commission's general rulemaking authority under PURA § 14.002. It opens no
   new subject. It completes a measurement framework already before the Commission by supplying the
   definitional sections — and the statutory basis for each — without which the framework cannot be applied
   uniformly.

   1.1 What is already before the Commission
   The authority and the obligation to measure large-load consumption are already codified. This petition
   operates entirely inside the existing statutory framework. It does not add new demands. It completes the
   definitions the framework requires in order to be enforceable, and it cites the statutes that already require
   them.

   The distinction matters procedurally. A petition asking the Commission to regulate something it has not
   been asked to regulate is a new subject. A petition supplying the operative definitions for a measurement
   the Commission is already directed to obtain is completion of an existing framework. This petition is the
   second kind. Every subsection proposed in Part V attaches to an obligation that already exists in statute,



GRUS · Petition for Adoption of a Rule · 16 TAC § 25.___ · PUC Project No. 60084                                    Page 2 of 33
    rule, or executive directive; none creates a new obligation, and none requires an instrument that Texas law
   has not already defined.

   1.2 The codified authority and obligation

   1.2.1 Senate Bill 6 and PURA § 37.0561
   Senate Bill 6 (89th Leg., R.S., 2025), effective June 20, 2025, enacted PURA § 37.0561, directing the
   Commission to establish interconnection standards for any new or expanded large load exceeding 75 MW
   at a single site, including demonstrated site control, disclosure obligations, and detailed site-related studies
   expressly including water studies with quarterly updates. SB 6 requires large loads to contribute the full
   cost of interconnection and directs Commission implementation by December 31, 2026.

   Two features of SB 6 matter directly. First, the statute already contemplates a water study as a recurring
   deliverable, not a one-time representation — which presupposes a measurement method capable of
   producing a comparable figure quarter over quarter. A figure not produced by a stated method against a
   stated boundary cannot be compared to the figure produced three months earlier, and a quarterly series of
   such figures records nothing. Second, the statute routes large-load disclosure through the transmission
   provider and the independent organization certified under PURA § 39.151, not through the load's own
   unverified statement. The rule proposed here supplies the water-side and electrical-side methods that make
   both features operable.

   1.2.2 The implementing rules
   16 TAC § 25.194, published for adoption March 12, 2026, implements SB 6's large-load interconnection
   standards for loads of 75 MW or greater. 16 TAC § 25.205, adopted March 2026, governs large-load
   interconnection and disclosure. The section proposed here is drafted to operate alongside § 25.194 and is
   proposed for placement adjacent to it.

   1.2.3 The survey and its documented failure
   The General Appropriations Act established a survey requiring data centers to report water and power
   usage. That self-reporting requirement produced compliance from fewer than ten percent of data centers.
   That documented failure is the stated basis of the Governor's directive described immediately below, and it
   is the empirical premise of Part II of this petition.

   1.2.4 The Governor's Directive of August 3, 2026
   The Governor's Directive of August 3, 2026 ordered the Commission and ERCOT to conduct a
   comprehensive verification and audit of all data centers in the ERCOT interconnection queue —
   approximately 474 GW of requests, roughly ninety percent attributable to data centers — including
   projected annual and peak water consumption, the water source, and the cooling technology, and to deny
   grid connection to non-compliant projects.

   The directive therefore already requires the three quantities this petition supplies methods for: a water
   consumption figure (annual and peak), an identified and legally authorized source, and a stated cooling
   technology. What the directive does not, and by its nature cannot, specify is how those three quantities are
   to be measured, by whom, against what facility class, and in what form the result is transmitted to the
   several authorities that need it. Those are engineering and definitional questions, and they are the subject
   of Part V.

   1.2.5 Water metering authority already exists
   Texas Water Code Ch. 13, Subch. M and 16 TAC Ch. 24, Subch. I (including § 24.283) codify point-of-use
   submetering — a meter placed downstream of a master meter to measure a defined use. The concept, the
   instrument, and the regulatory recognition all exist. The proposed rule applies that codified concept to a


GRUS · Petition for Adoption of a Rule · 16 TAC § 25.___ · PUC Project No. 60084                           Page 3 of 33
    defined point: the feed to an evaporative circuit.

   1.2.6 The system-integrity floors already exist
   Texas public water systems are bound by both a design standard and an operating standard:

        30 TAC § 290.44(d) — the distribution system must be designed to maintain a minimum pressure of
        35 psi at all points within the distribution network at flow rates of at least 1.5 gallons per minute per
        connection, and, where the system provides firefighting capability, to maintain at least 20 psi under
        combined fire and drinking-water flow conditions.

        30 TAC § 290.46(r) — all public water systems must be operated to provide a minimum pressure of 35
        psi throughout the distribution system under normal operating conditions, and to maintain at least 20
        psi during emergencies such as firefighting.

        30 TAC § 290.45 — minimum system capacity requirements, including source, service-pump, and
        storage capacity, stated per connection by system category (for example, elevated storage of 100
        gallons per connection for systems above 2,500 connections, or a pressure-tank capacity of 20 gallons
        per connection within the limits stated in the rule).

   The design floor and the operating floor are distinct obligations, and both are relevant. A distribution
   system may have been lawfully designed to 35 psi years before a large evaporative load appeared on it, and
   still fail the operating requirement of § 290.46(r) once that load is added at coincident summer peak. A
   measurement standard that produces the added consumptive draw at the point and time it occurs is what
   allows either obligation to be evaluated before the failure rather than after it.

   1.3 The four specifications the framework does not yet contain
   The audit is mandatory and the metering concept is codified. What the framework does not yet specify is:

    1. The measurement boundary — the physical point at which water and electrical consumption are
        read. Proposed subsection (f) on the water leg; subsection (i) on the electrical leg.

    2. Who is competent to verify it — the qualification and independence of the party whose reading the
        State relies upon. Proposed subsection (g).

    3. The facility classes it must read — the workload and cooling classifications that determine which
        measurement method applies and against which peak the facility is assessed. Proposed subsections (d),
        (e), and (h).

    4. How its output resolves jurisdiction — the single standardized record readable by every authority
        with jurisdiction over a component of the site's draw, together with the realized-figure and cost-
        causation consequences that follow. Proposed subsections (j), (k), and (l).

   1.4 What this petition does not do
   For clarity of the record, and to narrow what the Commission must decide:

        It does not propose a new instrument. Every meter specified is an off-the-shelf device already used
        for revenue billing or tenant allocation in Texas.

        It does not propose inspection of software, source code, model weights, customer algorithms, or
        tenant data. Measurement operates only on detectable physical electrical, thermal, and hydraulic
        quantities. Proposed subsection (b)(4) states this as an operative limit of the rule.

        It does not propose a cap, a moratorium, a siting restriction, or a denial standard. It proposes
        measurement. What the State does with a measured figure is the State's determination.



GRUS · Petition for Adoption of a Rule · 16 TAC § 25.___ · PUC Project No. 60084                          Page 4 of 33
         It does not name, target, or evaluate any operator. Every figure used is drawn from published
        vendor-neutral specifications.

        It does not seek any exclusive role for Petitioner, or for any vendor, utility, or verifier, in performing
        the measurement it proposes.

        It does not propose a remedy, a threshold, or a penalty. Those are governmental determinations
        belonging to the bodies holding the applicable statutory authority. Petitioner does not hold that
        authority and does not seek it. Nothing in § 22.281(a)(1) requires a petition for a measurement rule to
        propose one.



         PART II — WHY SELF-REPORTING IS INSUFFICIENT AS A MATTER OF
                                  RECORD,
                AND WHY THIRD-PARTY VERIFICATION IS REQUIRED


   2.1 Self-reporting has already failed in this exact context, on the record
   The General Appropriations Act survey measuring data-center water and power usage produced
   compliance from fewer than ten percent of data centers. That documented failure is the stated basis of the
   Governor's August 3, 2026 audit directive.

   The significance is not that the compliance rate was low. It is that the failure was method failure, not
   enforcement failure. The survey asked the measured party to produce its own figure. Fewer than one in ten
   produced anything at all, and for those that did, the State received an assertion whose accuracy it had no
   independent means to test. A standard that permits the measured party to produce its own unverified
   figure repeats the precise failure the audit was ordered to cure — and does so at a moment when roughly
   474 GW of interconnection requests are pending on the answer.

   2.2 No other regulated connection to shared public infrastructure is certified by the connecting
   party's own word
   An electrical interconnection is inspected and verified independently. A plumbing tie-in to a public water
   system is inspected and verified independently. A commercial revenue meter is set, sealed, and read by the
   utility, not by the customer. Elevators, boilers, fire-suppression systems, and structural welds in this state
   are all verified by a party other than the one whose work is being verified.

   The integrity principle is uniform across Texas utility regulation: the party consuming a shared public
   resource does not self-certify its own consumption. SB 6 itself embodies this — it routes large-load
   disclosures through the transmission provider and the independent organization certified under PURA §
   39.151, not through the load's unverified self-statement. The water measurement should follow the same
   principle the electrical measurement already follows.

   Stated as a question the Commission can answer directly: if the electrical interconnection of a 75 MW load
   is not accepted on the applicant's own word, there is no principled reason the water consumption of the
   same load at the same site on the same day should be.

   2.3 The requirement stated
   The standard must require independent third-party measurement or verification. The measurement shall be
   performed by, or verified by, a qualified party independent of the entity being measured, in accordance
   with the specifications proposed in Part V. The requirement is not satisfied by a figure produced solely by
   the entity being measured.



GRUS · Petition for Adoption of a Rule · 16 TAC § 25.___ · PUC Project No. 60084                           Page 5 of 33
    Two elements of that sentence are load-bearing and are defined precisely in Part V. Qualified is defined by
   reference to the independence-of-judgment standard already codified in Texas law (Part III and proposed
   subsection (g)) — not by any new licensing scheme, registry, or certification program, none of which
   presently exists for this field and none of which this petition asks the Commission to create. In accordance
   with the specifications proposed means the verifier reads the boundaries defined in proposed subsections
   (f) and (i), against the classification defined in subsections (d), (e), and (h), and reports in the form defined
   in subsection (j). A verification performed against no stated method is not a verification; it is a second
   assertion.

   2.4 The cost of the alternative
   If the standard permits self-reported figures, three consequences follow mechanically, and each is
   presently observable in the record:

    1. The figure is unfalsifiable. No reviewing agency can distinguish a conservative estimate from an
        optimistic one, because no physical reading exists against which either can be checked.

    2. Cost causation cannot be enforced. PURA § 35.004(c-1) assigns interconnection and infrastructure
        cost to the load that causes it. Assignment requires a measured quantity of causation. Without one, the
        default is socialization onto the general rate base — the outcome the statute was enacted to prevent.

    3. Failures surface only physically. A municipal system that cannot hold 35 psi under a new coincident
        load does not announce the fact administratively. It announces it as a pressure complaint, a brown-
        water event, or a boil-water notice, after the fact, to residents who had no part in the transaction.



                 PART III — THE INDEPENDENCE-OF-JUDGMENT STANDARD
                                 ALREADY IN TEXAS LAW


   3.1 Texas already codifies the standard that governs who may verify a measurement
   Texas does not need a new definition of a competent verifier. It already has one, and the operative quality it
   names is independence of judgment. Under the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation's rules for
   industrialized housing and buildings, a third-party inspection agency is an approved person or entity
   determined to be qualified by reason of facilities, personnel, experience, demonstrated reliability,
   and independence of judgment to inspect work for compliance with approved plans, documentation, the
   compliance-control program, and the applicable code. The individual third-party inspector is defined in
   parallel terms.

   Citation note: this definition is cited by TDLR as 16 TAC § 70.10(a)(39) in its Third Party Inspector Information Packet; in
   the currently published text of the rule the corresponding definitions appear at 16 TAC § 70.10(a) (third party inspection
   agency; third party inspector; third party site inspector). The Commission should read the citation as being to the definition,
   which has been stable in substance, rather than to a paragraph number that has moved with amendment. This petition cites
   it as 16 TAC § 70.10(a) throughout, retaining the (a)(39) reference where the TDLR packet is the source.

   The structure of that definition is worth stating plainly, because it is the structure the measurement
   standard borrows: verification of compliance is entrusted to a party independent of the party whose work is
   being verified, precisely because independence of judgment is the quality that makes a verification reliable.
   Facilities, personnel, experience, and demonstrated reliability establish that the verifier can measure.
   Independence of judgment establishes that the measurement can be relied upon.

   3.2 A self-report cannot meet that standard
   A data center's self-report of its own consumption cannot meet the standard, and the reason is definitional



GRUS · Petition for Adoption of a Rule · 16 TAC § 25.___ · PUC Project No. 60084                                          Page 6 of 33
    rather than reputational. The measured party is not independent of the measurement; it has a direct
   interest in the result. A figure produced by the party being measured therefore lacks the independence of
   judgment that Texas law already requires of a verification, and is an assertion rather than a verified
   measurement. No inference of bad faith is required to reach that conclusion, and none is offered here. The
   point is structural: the same figure produced by an interested party and by a disinterested party are not the
   same evidentiary object, and Texas law has already decided which one a verification is.

   3.3 The approval criteria are also already written
   Texas law goes further than defining independence; it states operationally what an independent verifier
   must attest. Under 16 TAC § 70.23(b)(4), an agency seeking approval must submit a signed statement that,
   among other things:

        its board, as a body, and its managerial and inspection personnel, as individuals, are free to exercise
        independence of judgment in the performance of their duties;

        its activities in discharging its responsibilities will not result in financial benefit via stock ownership or
        other financial interest in any producer, supplier, or vendor of the products involved, other than
        through standard fees for services rendered;

        it will consistently and uniformly implement the governing interpretations of the standards and rules;
        and

        it will not provide design services for the party whose work it inspects.

   Every one of those four attestations transposes directly onto the measurement proposed here, and the
   fourth is the most important. A party that designed the cooling plant, specified the misting skid, or
   engineered the electrical distribution is not positioned to verify the consumption of what it designed. The
   standard proposed in subsection (g) adopts these criteria by reference rather than inventing new ones,
   which has the additional advantage that a Texas verifier already knows what the attestation means.

   3.4 This is not a new or special rule for data centers
   It is the same standard applied to the same kind of question. The Governor's August 3, 2026 directive
   orders an audit — a verification — of data-center consumption. An audit ordered by the State falls within
   the same scope that makes verification of compliance a matter of independent judgment throughout Texas
   regulation. The self-reporting method already failed on the record (Part II); the reason it cannot be relied
   upon is the reason Texas law already gives — a party cannot supply the independent judgment required to
   verify its own compliance.


      Terminology adopted throughout this petition. This petition uses qualified independent third
      party, and never certified third party. The distinction is deliberate and material: there is at present no
      certification,    license,    or   registry    specific    to   computational-load   and   evaporative-consumption
      measurement in Texas, and a rule that required one would be unenforceable on the day it was adopted.
      Qualified is a substantive test the Commission or the receiving authority applies to a given party
      against the criteria in subsection (g) — facilities, personnel, experience, demonstrated reliability,
      independence of judgment, and the absence of a design or financial relationship with the measured
      entity. It is satisfiable today, by licensed professional engineers, testing and metering firms, and
      independent inspection agencies already operating in this state.




        PART IV — THE CLASSIFICATION FRAMEWORK: ENGINEERING BASIS



GRUS · Petition for Adoption of a Rule · 16 TAC § 25.___ · PUC Project No. 60084                                   Page 7 of 33
    Measurement without classification is not uniform. Two facilities drawing the same annual kilowatt-hours
   can impose radically different physical strain on grid and water infrastructure depending on the shape of
   the load and the method used to reject its heat. Part IV establishes the two axes against which any facility
   is read, and it does so entirely from published, vendor-neutral figures so that the framework can be applied
   by any reviewer without access to proprietary data. The classification stated in this Part is adopted as
   operative rule text at proposed subsections (d) and (e).


   IV.A Hardware Sourcing and Device-Level Reference Draw

   To establish a neutral, non-arbitrary baseline for classification, the standard relies entirely on published,
   vendor-neutral device thermal design power (TDP) specifications:

    Device class                                  Published reference draw              Note

    Standard server CPU (dual-socket)             150–250 W per chip                    Approximately 600–750 W per standard server
                                                                                        unit including platform overhead

    Prior-generation AI GPU (A100 class)          ~400 W per unit                       Board power

    Current-generation AI GPU (H100               ~700 W per unit                       Board power
    class)

    Next-generation AI GPU                        1,200–1,400 W per unit                Projected roadmap TDP

    High-bandwidth memory (HBM) stack             10–15 W per stack                     6–12 stacks per high-performance GPU

    Integrated 8-GPU server                       ~5.6 kW GPU-only; 6.5–7.5             Expanded figure accounts for CPU, memory,
                                                  kW per server                         and network overhead


   These are not Petitioner's figures and are not offered as such. They are published manufacturer
   specifications, and the reference panel schedule at Exhibit 4 is populated from them so that any reviewer
   can reconstruct the panel independently. Under proposed subsection (k)(1), a published TDP is a legitimate
   input to a Designed or Modeled figure and is never, standing alone, a Measured one.


   IV.B Density Classes, Cooling Regimes, and the Physical Air-Cooling Limit

   Using the device-level baselines above, five rack density classes map directly onto their engineering cooling
   requirements:

    Facility / rack class                            Rack density                  Required cooling regime

    Traditional enterprise / storage / web           5–15 kW per rack              Conventional air cooling (CRAC / CRAH units)

    Mixed / general compute                          15–30 kW per rack             Air cooling pushed to its thermal limit; containment
                                                                                   and elevated airflow required

    AI inference                                     20–40 kW per rack             Transition zone: rear-door liquid heat exchangers
                                                                                   or localized cold plates


    AI training                                      40–80 kW per rack             Direct liquid cooling (DLC) or cold plates required

    Next-generation AI                               150+ kW per rack              Advanced DLC, cold plates, or full immersion
                                                                                   cooling


   The physical threshold. Air-cooling infrastructure reaches a hard physical limit at approximately 25–30
   kW per rack. Beyond this density, liquid cooling is a strict physical necessity dictated by thermodynamic
   and airflow limits, not a flexible design preference. The consequence for classification is direct: a facility


GRUS · Petition for Adoption of a Rule · 16 TAC § 25.___ · PUC Project No. 60084                                                  Page 8 of 33
    that states a rack density above roughly 30 kW and simultaneously claims a purely air-cooled configuration
   has stated two things that cannot both be true, and the filing is deficient on its face under proposed
   subsection (k)(1)(C).


   IV.C The Deterministic Heat-and-Water Chain

   Data-center energy use is not an abstract metric. It is a physical event connected to local grid and water
   infrastructure through a deterministic three-link chain. Each link is an identity or a bounded engineering
   ratio, not an assumption, and each is derived with worked arithmetic in Annex I.

   IV.C.1 Link one — electrical draw to heat
   Computational silicon performs no mechanical work and stores no significant energy. Essentially all
   electrical power delivered to it is converted to heat:

     Q [BTU/hr] = P [W] × 3.412142            equivalently      Q [BTU/hr] = P [MW] × 3,412,142


   This is a unit identity, not a model. A 150 kW rack rejects 511,821 BTU/hr — approximately 42.7 tons of
   refrigeration at the 12,000 BTU/hr refrigeration ton, or the continuous output of roughly five to six typical
   residential furnaces rated at 80,000–100,000 BTU/hr input.

   IV.C.2 Link two — heat to cooling energy
   Removing that thermal energy requires cooling power. In high-density operations, cooling and facility
   overhead account for approximately 30–40 percent of total facility electricity; air cooling demands roughly
   an additional 0.3–0.5 W of cooling power for every 1 W of active IT load. Expressed as power usage
   effectiveness:

     Ptotal facility = PIT × PUE      where PUE ≈ 1.15–1.25 (dry, mild) to 1.50–1.70+ (extreme ambient)


   The reported electrical figure must therefore be the gross facility figure. Reporting critical IT load alone
   understates the physical draw on the grid by the entire cooling and infrastructure fraction — which is to
   say, by exactly the fraction that grows during the summer hours when the grid is most constrained.

   IV.C.3 Link three — cooling to water consumption
   Where heat is rejected evaporatively, water is consumed by phase change. The consumed mass follows
   from the latent heat of vaporization:

     mwater [lb/hr] = Q [BTU/hr] ÷ hfg          Vwater [gal/hr] = mwater ÷ 8.34
     At hfg ≈ 1,050 BTU/lb (typical of tower operating temperatures):
     1 MW of heat rejected evaporatively = 3,412,142 ÷ 1,050 ÷ 8.34 = 389.6 gal/hr = 9,352 gal/MW-day


   Two independent methods agree on this figure. The latent-heat derivation above gives approximately 390
   gal/hr per MW. The cooling-tower rule of thumb — evaporation of approximately one percent of
   recirculating flow per 10°F of range — gives 409 gal/hr per MW. The consumptive evaporation rate for a
   fully evaporative facility is therefore approximately 390–410 gal/hr per MW of heat rejected, and this
   petition uses 390 gal/hr per MW as the working value.

   Evaporation is not the whole of the water draw. Total makeup water fed to an evaporative circuit is the sum
   of evaporation, drift, and blowdown:

     Makeup = Evaporation + Drift + Blowdown                Blowdown = Evaporation ÷ (COC − 1)


GRUS · Petition for Adoption of a Rule · 16 TAC § 25.___ · PUC Project No. 60084                          Page 9 of 33
      Makeup = Evaporation × COC ÷ (COC − 1)                 where COC = cycles of concentration


    Cycles of                   Evaporation (gal/hr        Blowdown (gal/hr        Total makeup (gal/hr   Total makeup
    concentration (COC)         per MW)                    per MW)                 per MW)                (gal/MW-day)

    3 cycles                    390                        195                     584                    14,027

    4 cycles                    390                        130                     520                    12,469

    5 cycles                    390                        97                      487                    11,689

    6 cycles                    390                        78                      468                    11,222

    8 cycles                    390                        56                      445                    10,687


   Drift from a modern tower with drift eliminators is bounded at roughly 0.005 percent of recirculating flow
   and is negligible in volume, but it is not negligible in kind: drift is consumptive loss to atmosphere and,
   unlike blowdown, does not return to the collection system.


      Why this distinction governs the rule text. Blowdown is discharged to the sanitary sewer — it is
      withdrawn but not consumed, and it reappears downstream as a high-salinity load on the wastewater
      plant. Evaporation and drift are consumed to atmosphere and do not reappear anywhere. A single
      intake figure at the property line cannot distinguish the two, which is precisely why proposed
      subsection (f) requires a secondary meter on the evaporative feed rather than a larger primary meter
      at the fence.


   IV.C.4 Worked illustration at facility scale
   A facility with 100 MW of IT load operating at a PUE of 1.4 draws 140 MW gross and rejects approximately
   478 million BTU/hr. If that heat is rejected entirely evaporatively, consumptive evaporation is
   approximately 1.31 million gallons per day, before blowdown. At four cycles of concentration, total
   makeup is approximately 1.75 MGD. A single 150 kW AI rack, by the same arithmetic, evaporates
   approximately 1,400 gallons per day and requires approximately 1,700–2,100 gallons per day of makeup
   depending on cycles — comparable to the daily water demand of roughly eight to ten suburban households.

   These illustrations are stated as Modeled figures under proposed subsection (k)(1), derived from published ratios and stated

   IV.D Axis 1 — Workload Profile Classification (Classes W-1, W-2, W-3)

   Axis 1 classifies a facility, or a circuit within a facility, by the shape of its electrical load over time. Shape is
   the property that determines how much capacity a utility must hold in reserve, and it is the property that a
   time-averaged reading destroys.

   Class W-1 — Continuous High-Utilization (AI Training / HPC)
   Class W-1 defines computational workloads characterized by a high, flat, and uninterrupted electrical load
   shape. It represents the most energy-dense and thermally intense operational class in modern data-center
   infrastructure.

   1. Electrical load shape and utilization. Class W-1 workloads operate at 95 percent or greater sustained
   utilization for long, continuous execution runs, frequently measured in days or weeks. Unlike variable cloud

    or web traffic, the load shape does not fluctuate: the peak current draw and the average current draw are
   virtually identical throughout the job run.

   2. Hardware and power density. Class W-1 is typical of AI model-training superclusters — integrated 8-
   GPU nodes such as H100, H200, or B200 class systems — and of continuous high-performance computing.
   Rack power densities range from 40 to 80+ kW per rack, extending to 150+ kW per rack in next-generation
   architectures. An integrated 8-GPU server node alone draws 6.5 to 7.5 kW.

   3. Thermal and water footprint. Because computational silicon converts essentially all electrical input
   into heat, Class W-1 facilities produce continuous maximum heat rejection. Beyond the 25–30 kW per rack
   threshold, air cooling fails, making direct liquid cooling or cold plates physically mandatory. When paired
   with evaporative cooling towers, this continuous thermal output drives sustained, maximum municipal
   water consumption — on the order of 390 gal/hr per MW of rejected heat, continuously, for the duration of
   the run (Annex I).

   4. Measurement and regulatory rule. Because peak and average draw are nearly identical, Class W-1
   loads cannot be concealed behind time-averaging — but neither can they be understated by it. Class W-1
   circuits must be metered at the secondary distribution bus or PDU level (the M2 transport boundary) using
   revenue-grade current-transformer submeters compliant with ANSI C12.20 or IEC 62053-22, together with
   open server telemetry, so that continuous grid and thermal strain is accurately attributed to the circuits
   producing it.


      Why W-1 is the reference class for water. A continuous class has no diversity. There is no hour of
      the day in which a training cluster's heat rejection falls off, and therefore no hour in which its
      evaporative makeup demand falls off. Utility planning practice that assumes a load factor materially
      below unity is inapplicable to Class W-1, and a water study that applies one to a W-1 facility
      understates the demand by the inverse of the assumed factor.


   Class W-2 — Burst / Variable (AI Inference, Cloud, and Colocation)
   Class W-2 defines computational workloads whose power draw rises and falls dynamically with real-time
   user query volume and transactional demand. Unlike flat, continuous training runs, Class W-2 represents a
   highly non-uniform, bursty load profile that presents distinct challenges for grid and municipal water

   1. Electrical load shape and utilization dynamics.

        Demand-driven swings. Operating utilization swings rapidly between 40 percent and 100 percent of
        thermal design power based on real-time API query traffic, model inference requests, or cloud

        Peak-versus-average disparity. The instantaneous peak electrical draw far exceeds the long-term
        annual mean. Because queries cluster during business hours and active usage windows, Class W-2
        creates steep, high-amplitude power ramps against a lower nighttime baseline.

   2. Hardware architecture and rack density. Deployed across high-density GPU inference nodes,
   specialized ASIC accelerators, and multi-tenant cloud application servers, operating primarily in the 20 to
   40 kW per rack bracket. This is the physical transition zone where conventional air cooling reaches its
   thermodynamic limit (25–30 kW per rack), requiring rear-door liquid heat exchangers or localized cold
   plates to handle rapid thermal spikes.

   3. Thermal rejection and environmental strain.

   C-1 preserves municipal water, air-cooled chillers require higher electrical input per watt of IT load at high
   ambient temperature — typically 0.3 to 0.5 W of cooling power per 1 W of IT load — exchanging water
   consumption for higher peak electrical demand on the grid. Class C-1 is therefore not the costless

   Class C-2 — Closed-Loop / Recirculating Non-Evaporative
   Class C-2 defines cooling architectures using a sealed recirculating loop to transfer heat away from
   computational hardware without evaporating water to atmosphere.

   1. Core mechanics — the sealed loop. Class C-2 systems use sealed internal fluid loops (treated water,
   glycol, or dielectric fluid) running through liquid-to-liquid heat exchangers, rear-door heat exchangers, or
   direct liquid cooling cold plates mounted to CPU/GPU dies. Because the internal loop is sealed, water
   recirculates continuously with zero operational evaporation or blowdown discharge from that loop.

   2. The outdoor rejection condition — closing the C-2 / C-3 loophole. A closed indoor liquid loop is
   not, on its own, sufficient to claim Class C-2 status. Class C-2 holds only if heat rejection to the outside is
   also non-evaporative — dry fluid coolers or air-cooled radiators. If a facility uses a closed indoor liquid loop
   but rejects that heat outdoors using evaporative cooling towers, adiabatic wetted media, or spray ponds,
   the facility is not Class C-2. It is Class C-3, because the consumptive water loss occurs at the outdoor
   heat-rejection stage.

   3. Texas summer heat and the Class C-4 transition. During extreme Texas ambient dry-bulb heat,
   outdoor dry coolers often cannot reject heat from high-density racks within design approach. If a Class C-2
   facility engages any evaporative assist — spray misting, condenser-coil pre-cooling, or wetted adiabatic
   pads — the facility automatically changes class to Class C-4 for that circuit, and that circuit becomes
   immediately subject to the secondary point-of-use submeter under 16 TAC § 24.283 and Tex. Water Code

   Class C-3 — Evaporative / Cooling Towers / Adiabatic
   Class C-3 defines architectures where heat is rejected directly to atmosphere by evaporating water. It is
   the most water-consumptive cooling classification and the primary technical focus of the Two-Meter
   Method.

   1. Core mechanics and water loss. Class C-3 systems rely on open or closed-circuit cooling towers,
   evaporative condensers, wetted-media adiabatic systems, or spray ponds. Thermal energy is transferred to
   a water loop and rejected as water changes phase from liquid to vapor. Water loss is an unavoidable
   thermodynamic consequence of operation and consists of:

        Evaporative loss — water converted to vapor and lost to atmosphere (~390 gal/hr per MW rejected);

        Drift — entrained droplets carried out of the tower, bounded at roughly 0.005 percent of recirculating
        flow by drift eliminators, and consumptive;

        Blowdown / bleed-off — concentrated water discharged to sewer to prevent scale, equal to
        evaporation divided by (COC − 1), and withdrawn but not consumed.

   2. The outdoor heat-rejection rule (distinguishing C-2 from C-3). A common misconception is that a
   facility with closed indoor liquid loops — direct-to-chip cold plates or rear-door heat exchangers — is
   automatically a closed-loop facility. The standard establishes the opposite: classification is governed by
   where the evaporative water loss physically occurs. A closed indoor loop rejecting heat outdoors
   through evaporative towers or wetted media is Class C-3.

   3. The mandatory Two-Meter Method.

        Primary service-entrance meter — the standard utility master meter measuring total water intake
        delivered to the property line.

        Secondary point-of-use submeter — an ordinary, off-the-shelf water meter installed at the feed line
        entering the evaporative cooling tower or loop.

        Calculating consumptive loss — metering the evaporative feed directly identifies the water entering the
        evaporative circuit; the portion of that feed that does not return as metered or conductivity-derived
        blowdown is the quantity consumed to atmosphere. This eliminates reliance on fictional drain-line
        estimates.

   4. Statutory grounding and municipal system protection. The secondary meter requires no
   specialized or proprietary hardware; it is the point-of-use submeter authorized under 16 TAC § 24.283 and
   Texas Water Code Ch. 13, Subch. M. Large continuous evaporative draws can depress local water system
   pressures; metering Class C-3 feeds ensures the draw can be evaluated against the 35 psi design and
   operating floors and the capacity requirements of 30 TAC §§ 290.44(d), 290.45, and 290.46(r).

   IV.G Workload Separation: Uniformity as the Decisive Property

   The justification for moving the regulatory measurement boundary from the facility fence (M1) to the



GRUS · Petition for Adoption of a Rule · 16 TAC § 25.___ · PUC Project No. 60084                                             Page 17 of 33
    internal transport boundary (M2) is physical load uniformity.

   Uniform loads (steady state). General compute, database, storage, and transactional applications run at
   low, predictable, steady draws. Their flat thermal and electrical footprints integrate easily into standard
   utility forecasting, and an averaged reading describes them accurately.

   Non-uniform loads (volatile peaks). AI model training (95 percent or greater sustained utilization) and
   large-model inference (demand-driven fluctuation between 40 and 100 percent of TDP) create highly
   variable or continuously maximal draws whose peak is the planning-relevant quantity. For these, an
   averaged reading is not merely imprecise; it describes a facility that does not exist.

   The socialization gap. Standard fence meters average volatile, high-amplitude spikes over billing
   intervals. This hides the physical peaks that force the utility to build grid capacity, upgrade transmission
   transformers, and secure additional water capacity. The capacity is built and paid for regardless; the only
   question the averaging resolves is who pays. Where the causing load is invisible, the cost defaults to the
   general rate base.

   The resolution — M2 isolation. Transport-boundary meters resolve power draw per circuit at the
   internal power distribution unit level. As demonstrated by drawing GRUS-GRID-005 (Exhibit 4), on a single
   reference PDU panel, four non-uniform AI circuits of eight total circuits drive approximately 168 A of
   approximately 256 A of peak draw and approximately 115 kWth of approximately 142.5 kWth of heat — and
   therefore the corresponding majority of cooling-water consumption — while general compute, database,
   and storage circuits draw a small, steady, uniform fraction. The aggregate fence meter sees only the
   summed current and cannot resolve that four circuits are responsible. The M2 meter resolves it per circuit.

   Drawing GRUS-GRID-001 (Exhibit 1) establishes why this is not an arbitrary point of insertion: the same
   distribution hierarchy, the same step-down stages, and the same measurement-node structure recur at
   every scale from generation to the processor die. M2 is not a new kind of node invented for this rule;
   it is the same kind of node as M1, placed one level in.

   What resolution does and does not conclude. The panel schedule resolves where physical strain concentrates. It does not
   conclude that any facility should be denied service, curtailed, or charged a particular rate. Those are determinations for the
   Commission and the affected utilities on a measured record. Petitioner supplies the measurement; the State draws the
   conclusion.

      (d) Facility classification — workload axis.

      (1) Each computational facility, and each circuit within a computational facility, shall be classified on
      the workload axis as Class W-1, Class W-2, or Class W-3.

      (2) Class W-1, continuous high utilization. A load is Class W-1 if it operates at sustained utilization
      of 95 percent or greater of its thermal design power for continuous execution intervals, such that its
      peak draw and its average draw over the interval are substantially equal.

      demand such that instantaneous peak draw materially exceeds the arithmetic mean draw over the
      reporting period.

      class. A Class W-3 facility is classified on the workload axis as the set of its constituent classes and not
      as a single class.

      (5) Assessment peak by workload class. A Class W-1 facility or circuit shall be assessed against its
      sustained continuous draw. A Class W-2 facility or circuit shall be assessed against its measured peak
      draw; an arithmetic mean over a month or a year does not satisfy the reporting requirement of this
      section for a Class W-2 load. A Class W-3 facility shall be assessed as the sum of its constituent classes
      resolved per circuit, per panelboard, or per pod, and not as a single blended average.

      and shall state the integration interval from which the peak was taken.

      (f) Water measurement boundary — two-meter method.

      (1) The measured boundary. Consumptive water loss at a computational facility shall be determined
      from two physical meters:

      (A) the primary master service meter at the property entrance, measuring total water intake; and

      blowdown and bleed-off discharged from that circuit, less any other metered return. Blowdown shall
      be determined by a discharge meter where one is installed, or from the measured cycles of
      concentration of the circuit.

      (3) Quantities reported. Total intake, evaporative feed, and consumptive loss shall each be reported.
      Blowdown volume and the concentration of its constituents shall be reported to the authority receiving
      wastewater discharge under subsection (j)(1)(D) of this section.

      (4) Scope of coverage. The secondary submeter required by paragraph (1)(B) of this subsection shall
      meter the feed to any circuit that evaporates water rather than returning it, including a Class C-3
      circuit, a Class C-4 assist circuit, and a Class C-5 generation circuit. The obligation attaches to the
      circuit, not to the facility's stated classification, and attaches upon installation or first operation,

       whichever occurs earlier.

      (5) No novel instrument. The secondary submeter is a point-of-use submeter of the kind recognized
      under Texas Water Code, Chapter 13, Subchapter M, and § 24.283 of this title. No specialized or
      proprietary instrument is required. Meters shall be sized, installed, and maintained in accordance with
      applicable American Water Works Association standards and shall be calibrated at intervals not
      exceeding those the serving utility applies to comparable revenue meters.

      (6) Point of measurement. The quantity measured under paragraph (1)(B) of this subsection is the
      water fed into the evaporative circuit. Water entering that circuit and not returning is the water
      consumed to atmosphere. Nothing in this subsection requires the metering of water vapor or the
      estimation of a drain-line quantity.


   Basis. A single intake figure at the property line does not measure consumption, because a substantial
   portion of drawn water is returned to the sanitary sewer and only the evaporated fraction is consumed. It is
   the non-returned fraction — not intake — that determines whether the supplying system's pressure and
   capacity floors remain satisfied under the added load.

   The three reported quantities at paragraph (3) are not redundant. Total intake is what the supplying
   utility must deliver, and is the figure relevant to source, treatment, and pumping capacity. Evaporative
   feed is what must be delivered at the moment of ambient peak, and is the figure relevant to distribution
   pressure. Consumptive loss is what never comes back, and is the figure relevant to basin, aquifer, and
   regional planning. Blowdown is the figure relevant to the wastewater plant, because it returns
   concentrated in dissolved solids. One number cannot serve four authorities; three metered quantities can
   serve all four.

   Answering the principal engineering objection. The principal objection to water measurement at
   computational facilities is that consumptive loss cannot be metered because evaporation leaves no stream
   to meter. The objection is correct about the vapor and irrelevant to the method. Evaporation is measured
   by difference at the feed, in the same way any consumptive process is measured: by metering what goes in
   and accounting for what comes back out. Cycles of concentration are determined by conductivity, an
   ordinary and continuously logged tower measurement, which is why the return fraction is a determinable
   quantity rather than an assumption. Paragraphs (2) and (6) state one method, not two: (2) gives the
   arithmetic and (6) states the physical point of measurement and forecloses the drain-line objection.

   Relation to the system-integrity floors. The measurement required by this subsection is the quantity
   necessary to evaluate compliance with 30 TAC § 290.44(d) (design: minimum 35 psi at all points at flow
   rates of at least 1.5 gpm per connection; 20 psi under combined fire and drinking-water flow), 30 TAC §
   290.46(r) (operation: minimum 35 psi under normal operating conditions; 20 psi during emergencies such
   as firefighting), and 30 TAC § 290.45 (minimum system capacity). Absent a secondary evaporative meter,
   compliance with those floors can only be asserted, and failure surfaces only when a smaller system is
   physically overtaxed. The design floor and the operating floor are separate obligations and fail in different
   ways: a system lawfully designed to 35 psi at 1.5 gpm per connection may still fall below 35 psi in operation
   once a continuous multi-hundred-gallon-per-hour evaporative draw is added at a single node during a
   coincident summer peak, because the design case did not contemplate that node. This subsection produces
   the input to the hydraulic evaluation of that case. It does not itself determine compliance; it makes
   determination possible.

   authorities are addressed in terms of availability rather than directive. The practical effect is that a facility

                PART VI — WHY THESE BELONG INSIDE THE MEASUREMENT


   6.1 Each subsection specifies the measurement itself
   Each proposed subsection specifies a necessary element of the measurement: what it measures on the
   water leg (subsection (f), the secondary evaporative meter and the Two-Meter Method) and on the
   electrical leg (subsection (i), the two-tier bus submeter and existing telemetry); who verifies it (subsection
   (g), a qualified party independent of the one being measured); the class it reads (subsections (d), (e), and
   (h), the two-axis profile); what its reading resolves (subsection (j), the jurisdiction); the evidentiary grade
   and scope of what is reported (subsection (k)); and the allocation the reading supports (subsection (l)).

   Remove any one and the standard cannot be applied uniformly. Without a boundary, two verifiers measure
   different things. Without a verifier standard, the boundary is read by an interested party. Without
   classification, the same reading means different things at different facilities. Without a common record,
   four authorities receive four partial answers. Without evidence grades, a projection and a measurement
   appear identical on the page. Without allocation, a correct measurement produces no consequence. These
   are the definitions the framework already requires in order to function, each grounded in a standard or
   statute already in force.

   6.2 The burden is minimal and the method is ordinary
   On the water leg: one commonplace point-of-use water meter at a defined point, added to a facility that
   already has a primary meter and is already required by SB 6 to submit water studies and to bear

   interest in protecting.

   What it produces is the one quantity presently missing and unverifiable: how much water and how much
   peak power a large load actually consumes, measured at the point it occurs, verified by a party competent
   and independent enough to measure it, assessed against the correct facility class.

   6.3 What the whole converts
   Taken together, these subsections convert the mandated audit from a self-report the facility fills out — the
   method that already failed at better than ninety percent — into a measurement the State can stand behind:
   measured at a defined boundary by an ordinary secondary meter and standard bus submeters, verified by a
   qualified independent party, assessed against a stated facility class, and recorded in a form every affected
   authority can read.

   That is the entire proposal. It does not decide whether any facility should be built, connected, curtailed, or
   charged. It decides only that the quantities on which those decisions rest will be measured rather than
   asserted.

C.6 Core Forensic Rules for Heat-Transfer Boundary Audits
1. Governance by Q = UA ΔTlm. Increasing heat-exchanger surface area (A) reduces the approach temperature, but
   cannot alter or lower the ambient dry-bulb or wet-bulb floor. No quantity of equipment moves the ambient condition.
2. Rejection of fictional continuous limits. An absolute equipment limit of 125 °F or 135 °F cannot be treated as a
   recommended continuous operating temperature when the manufacturer specifies 108 °F. A filing that operates the
   design case at the absolute rating is deficient under § V.F.1.
3. Misting reduction verification. Misting or adiabatic pre-cooling cannot be claimed to produce a fixed 20 °F or 23 °F
   temperature drop without documented dry-bulb, wet-bulb, and relative-humidity test logs. The claimed drop shall be
   stated as a saturation effectiveness against the measured wet-bulb, and effectiveness above 0.90 shall be supported by
   manufacturer test data at the stated ambient condition.
4. The wet-bulb floor is absolute. Evaporative cooling of any kind — tower, adiabatic pad, or fogging skid — cannot
   produce an air or water temperature below the ambient wet-bulb. Any filing whose design case implies otherwise is
   deficient on its face.
5. Water follows heat, not nameplate. Consumptive water is a function of heat actually rejected evaporatively, not of
   installed capacity. A facility operating at 60 percent load evaporates approximately 60 percent of the design rate; a
   facility at continuous 95 percent utilization (Class W-1) does not.

B.2 Thermodynamic Heat and Water Performance Analysis

B.2.1 The 25–30 kW per Rack Limit and the Air-Cooling Threshold
Physical threshold. Air cooling (Class C-1) reaches a hard thermodynamic and airflow limit near 25–30 kW per rack.
Above this density, liquid cooling — cold plates or direct-to-chip, Class C-2 — becomes a physical necessity rather than a
design preference.
The 108 °F OEM limit. While equipment may carry an absolute maximum rating of 125–135 °F, major dry-cooler
manufacturers specify approximately 108 °F dry-bulb as the maximum recommended continuous operating temperature.
Above it, fan power rises sharply and heat-exchanger approach temperatures break down. Annex B shows why this matters
in Texas specifically: at 108 °F and 30 percent relative humidity, 28.0 °F of evaporative potential remains available, and a
facility can hold full load by engaging an assist — which is precisely the moment it becomes a Class C-4 facility and incurs
the obligation of § V.A.

B.2.2 Evaporative Water Consumption Dynamics
Latent heat conversion. Rejecting 1 MW of heat evaporatively requires 3,412,142 BTU/hr of latent capacity. At hfg ≈
1,050 BTU/lb this consumes approximately 390 gal/hr per MW — approximately 9,350 gallons per MW-day of pure
evaporation, before blowdown. Including blowdown at typical cycles of concentration, total makeup runs approximately
10,700–14,000 gallons per MW-day (Part IV.C.3).
A single 150 kW AI rack. Rejects 511,821 BTU/hr — approximately 42.7 tons of refrigeration, or the continuous output of
roughly five to six residential furnaces. Under full evaporative rejection it evaporates approximately 1,400 gallons per day
and requires approximately 1,700–2,100 gallons per day of makeup depending on cycles of concentration — comparable to
the daily water demand of roughly eight to ten suburban households, from a single rack.

B.2.3 The Multi-Day Sustained Heat-Wave Risk
Coincident infrastructure stress. Continuous 108 °F-plus heat waves force Class C-3 and Class C-4 systems to operate at
or near full evaporative capacity for 72 or more consecutive hours. Unlike a single-day peak, a multi-day event gives
municipal storage no overnight recovery window, because the facility's draw does not fall at night and residential irrigation
demand resumes each morning against depleted elevated storage.
Municipal main depletion. These high-volume, uninterrupted draws depress municipal distribution mains, risking failure
of the 35 psi design and operating floors under 30 TAC §§ 290.44(d) and 290.46(r), and, if pressure falls below 20 psi,
triggering the back-siphonage and public-notification consequences that follow under TCEQ rules.

B.2.4 Automatic Reclassification in Operation
The moment a facility claiming Class C-1 or Class C-2 status engages condenser misting, fogging, or spray pre-cooling to
survive high ambient dry-bulb heat, it reclassifies to Class C-4 under § V.C.2, and that circuit becomes subject to the
secondary point-of-use submeter under 16 TAC § 24.283 and Tex. Water Code Ch. 13, Subch. M. Annex B identifies the
ambient conditions at which this transition predictably occurs, which is why the transition can be audited rather than
merely asserted.

D.1 Key Operational Findings
1. The Class C-4 transition trigger. In the hot/dry case, dry coolers reach their sensible rejection threshold. Engaging
   spray misting or adiabatic media depresses entering air toward the wet-bulb, maintaining 100 percent IT load capacity
   — and automatically reclassifying the circuit to Class C-4, triggering mandatory point-of-use submetering under 16 TAC
   § 24.283. The facility keeps its load by spending municipal water, and the standard's only requirement is that
   the spending be measured.
2. Wet-bulb compression in humid conditions. In the hot/humid case, high relative humidity compresses the
   evaporative potential to as little as 2.5–9 °F. Evaporative efficiency collapses precisely when heat rejection is hardest,
   forcing centrifugal chillers to carry the load and driving cooling overhead to +0.55 W per 1 W of IT. Water use does not
   fall in this case; blowdown rises as cycles concentrate, and the electrical draw rises alongside it.
3. Multi-day extreme strain. During sustained 108 °F-plus conditions, high-density AI clusters consume up to roughly
   2,100 gallons per day per 150 kW rack of makeup water while simultaneously imposing their maximum electrical
   demand. The two peaks are coincident by construction, not by coincidence — both are driven by the same ambient
   condition on the same afternoon as peak residential demand.
4. There is no water-free option at extreme ambient. A facility that avoids evaporative water entirely pays for it in
   electrical overhead at PUE 1.5–1.7 during precisely the hours ERCOT is most constrained. The two axes trade against
   each other, and a measurement standard that reads only one of them can be satisfied by moving the burden to the other.

 E.4.2 The six-tier relationship classification
 The relationship between a facility's water draw and a system event must be classified under one of six defined categories,
 and never by timing alone:
 1. No demonstrated correlation — physical, hydraulic, or temporal evidence disproves any connection.
 2. Temporal correlation only — peak draw coincided in time, but modeling or distance demonstrates no hydraulic
    mechanism.

 3. Engineering correlation — hydraulic modeling shows that intake velocity created transients, scouring velocities, or
   head loss capable of contributing.
4. Probable contribution — calculations and physical evidence indicate high-volume pumping combined with existing
   pipe degradation to induce failure.
5. Confirmed cause — telemetry, transducer logs, and pipe failure analysis confirm that facility operation caused the
   pressure drop or failure.
6. Unresolved — the record lacks sufficient telemetry, meter data, or inspection to support a determination.

E.4.3 Hydraulic mechanisms
Scouring velocities and hydraulic transients. Rapid, un-ramped valve openings for cooling-tower makeup or high-
pressure adiabatic spray (Classes C-3 and C-4) cause sudden velocity spikes in distribution mains. High velocity scours iron
and manganese tuberculation from older pipe walls, discoloring water throughout the pressure zone.
Pressure floor breaches. Sustained evaporative makeup draws during peak summer can pull distribution pressure below
the 35 psi operating floor. Below 20 psi, back-siphonage risk rises and the applicable public-notification obligations attach.

  Why this protocol protects both directions. A rigorous incident protocol is as valuable to a well-run facility as to a
  municipality. Without submeter logs and a stated classification method, a facility located near an aging main will be
  blamed for every discolored-water call in its pressure zone, and will have no evidence with which to answer. With them,
  the six-tier classification distinguishes ordinary pipe aging from facility-induced strain on the record. Measurement is
  the only thing that makes exoneration possible.

  ANNEX F — STATUTORY AND REGULATORY RECONCILIATION
 Legal and regulatory reconciliation requires evaluating project facts against governing statutes, administrative codes,
 utility protocols, and executive directives — not against unverified developer claims or prewritten legal conclusions. Each

 F.1 The Ten-Point Legal Record Structure
 For every regulatory requirement evaluated, ten parameters are recorded:
 1. Statute or rule — the governing legislative act, administrative code, or agency directive.
 2. Exact citation — section, subsection, and paragraph.
 3. Current effective date — enactment or publication date.
 4. Official source — issuing agency or statutory volume.
 5. Applicable jurisdiction — the body with regulatory authority.
 6. Factual trigger — the physical, electrical, or hydrological threshold that activates the requirement.
 7. Project fact satisfying or failing the trigger — the verified data point evaluated against it.
 8. Amendment and procedural classification — one of: Amendment Clearly Required; Amendment Potentially Required;
    Agency Determination Required; No Amendment Identified; Insufficient Documentation.

F.5 Statutory Takeaways
1. Water submetering is already codified. The Two-Meter Method requires no new statutory authority. Texas already
   recognizes point-of-use submeters under 16 TAC § 24.283 and Texas Water Code Ch. 13, Subch. M. Applying that
   instrument to the evaporative feed produces the physical data needed to evaluate the 35 psi design and operating floors.
2. Independent verification is already defined. Rather than creating new administrative definitions, the rule adopts the
   independence-of-judgment standard at 16 TAC § 70.10(a) and the attestation criteria at § 70.23(b)(4). That supplies a
   legal mechanism to execute the Governor's audit directive and to cure the documented failure of self-reporting.
3. One statute drives both boundaries. PURA § 35.004(c-1) requires large loads to contribute to interconnection and
   infrastructure cost recovery. Measuring electrical draw at the M2 transport boundary with revenue-grade instruments
   supplies the resolution necessary to assign caused cost to the causing load, and to insulate residential and small-
   business ratepayers from it.

 ANNEX G — REGIONAL AGGREGATION AND CUMULATIVE STRAIN
Computational load and infrastructure audits must never be conducted in isolation. Evaluating a single facility alone
creates a false sense of security: a project requesting 50 MW of power or 0.5 MGD of water may appear manageable on its
own application, while the same request aggregated across regional infrastructure boundaries, alongside every other
committed and queued request, can overtax shared electric infrastructure, deplete aquifers, and collapse municipal
pressure zones.
Annex G establishes a multi-dimensional aggregation protocol to identify cumulative regional strain, prevent jurisdictional
arbitrage, and reconcile project demands against regional planning baselines.

   THE INDISCRIMINATE READING — A FEW WORKLOAD CLASSES DRIVE MOST OF THE STRAIN
   Across the full landscape, the meter reads every class the same way. The result is not uniform: circuits 1–17 (AI training + large-model inference) carry the great
   majority of peak draw (~168 of ~256 A) and heat (~115 of ~142.5 kW), and therefore the great majority of cooling-water consumption — while general compute,
   database, and storage (circuits 23–33) are a small, steady, uniform fraction. On one panel, four circuits produce most of the physical strain on grid and water.

   The aggregate fence meter sees only the ~256 A sum and cannot resolve that four circuits are responsible. The transport-boundary meter (M2) resolves it per
   circuit. That resolution — indiscriminate across all classes, revealing where strain concentrates — is the entire purpose of the meter. GRUS draws no conclusion; the State does.

                             PART I - PURPOSE AND STATUTORY FRAME

   Procedural posture. This petition requests adoption of a rule of general applicability under Tex. Gov't
   Code § 2001.021 and the Commission's general rulemaking authority under PURA § 14.002. It opens no
   new subject. It completes a measurement framework already before the Commission by supplying the
   definitional sections - and the statutory basis for each - without which the framework cannot be applied
   uniformly.

   1.1 What is already before the Commission
   The authority and the obligation to measure large-load consumption are already codified. This petition
   operates entirely inside the existing statutory framework. It does not add new demands. It completes the
   definitions the framework requires in order to be enforceable, and it cites the statutes that already require
   them.

   The distinction matters procedurally. A petition asking the Commission to regulate something it has not
   been asked to regulate is a new subject. A petition supplying the operative definitions for a measurement
   the Commission is already directed to obtain is completion of an existing framework. This petition is the
   second kind. Every subsection proposed in Part V attaches to an obligation that already exists in statute,



GRUS · Petition for Adoption ofa Rule · 16 TAC § 25.- PUC Project No. 60084                                       Page 2 of 33
    rule, or executive directive; none creates a new obligation, and none requires an instrument that Texas law
   has not already defined.

   1.2 The codified authority and obligation

   1.2.1 Senate Bill 6 and PURA § 37.0561
   Senate Bill 6 (89th Leg., R. S., 2025), effective June 20, 2025, enacted PURA § 37.0561, directing the
   Commission to establish interconnection standards for any new or expanded large load exceeding 75 MW
   at a single site, including demonstrated site control, disclosure obligations, and detailed site-related studies
   expressly including water studies with quarterly updates. SB 6 requires large loads to contribute the full
   cost of interconnection and directs Commission implementation by December 31, 2026.

   Two features of SB 6 matter directly. First, the statute already contemplates a water study as a recurring
   deliverable, not a one-time representation - which presupposes a measurement method capable of
   producing a comparable figure quarter over quarter. A figure not produced by a stated method against a
   stated boundary cannot be compared to the figure produced three months earlier, and a quarterly series of
   such figures records nothing. Second, the statute routes large-load disclosure through the transmission
   provider and the independent organization certified under PURA § 39.151, not through the load's own
   unverified statement. The rule proposed here supplies the water-side and electrical-side methods that make
   both features operable.

   1.2.2 The implementing rules
   16 TAC § 25.194, published for adoption March 12, 2026, implements SB 6's large-load interconnection
   standards for loads of 75 MW or greater. 16 TAC § 25.205, adopted March 2026, governs large-load
   interconnection and disclosure. The section proposed here is drafted to operate alongside § 25.194 and is
   proposed for placement adjacent to it.

   1.2.3 The survey and its documented failure
   The General Appropriations Act established a survey requiring data centers to report water and power
   usage. That self-reporting requirement produced compliance from fewer than ten percent of data centers.
   That documented failure is the stated basis of the Governor's directive described immediately below, and it
   is the empirical premise of Part II of this petition.

   1.2.4 The Governor's Directive of August 3, 2026
   The Governor's Directive of August 3, 2026 ordered the Commission and ERCOT to conduct a
   comprehensive verification and audit of all data centers in the ERCOT interconnection queue -
   approximately 474 GW of requests, roughly ninety percent attributable to data centers - including
   projected annual and peak water consumption, the water source, and the cooling technology, and to deny
   grid connection to non-compliant projects.

   The directive therefore already requires the three quantities this petition supplies methods for: a water
   consumption figure (annual and peak), an identified and legally authorized source, and a stated cooling
   technology. What the directive does not, and by its nature cannot, specify is how those three quantities are
   to be measured, by whom, against what facility class, and in what form the result is transmitted to the
   several authorities that need it. Those are engineering and definitional questions, and they are the subject
   of Part V.

   1.2.5 Water metering authority already exists
   Texas Water Code Ch. 13, Subch. M and 16 TAC Ch. 24, Subch. I (including § 24.283) codify point-of-use
   submetering - a meter placed downstream of a master meter to measure a defined use. The concept, the
   instrument, and the regulatory recognition all exist. The proposed rule applies that codified concept to a


GRUS · Petition for Adoption ofa Rule · 16 TAC § 25.- PUC Project No. 60084                                 Page 3 of 33
    defined point: the feed to an evaporative circuit.

   1.2.6 The system-integrity floors already exist
   Texas public water systems are bound by both a design standard and an operating standard:

     • 30 TAC § 290.44(d) -the distribution system must be designed to maintain a minimum pressure of
        35 psi at all points within the distribution network at flow rates of at least 1.5 gallons per minute per
        connection, and, where the system provides firefighting capability, to maintain at least 20 psi under
        combined fire and drinking-water flow conditions.
     • 30 TAC § 290.46(r) - all public water systems must be operated to provide a minimum pressure of 35
        psi throughout the distribution system under normal operating conditions, and to maintain at least 20
        psi during emergencies such as firefighting.
     • 30 TAC § 290.45 - minimum system capacity requirements, including source, service-pump, and
        storage capacity, stated per connection by system category (for example, elevated storage of 100
        gallons per connection for systems above 2,500 connections, or a pressure-tank capacity of 20 gallons
        per connection within the limits stated in the rule).

   The design floor and the operating floor are distinct obligations, and both are relevant. A distribution
   system may have been lawfully designed to 35 psi years before a large evaporative load appeared on it, and
   still fail the operating requirement of § 290.46(r) once that load is added at coincident summer peak. A
   measurement standard that produces the added consumptive draw at the point and time it occurs is what
   allows either obligation to be evaluated before the failure rather than after it.

   1.3 The four specifications the framework does not yet contain
   The audit is mandatory and the metering concept is codified. What the framework does not yet specify is:

   figure repeats the precise failure the audit was ordered to cure - and does so at a moment when roughly

   2.2 No other regulated connection to shared public infrastructure is certified by the connecting
   party's own word
   An electrical interconnection is inspected and verified independently. A plumbing tie-in to a public water
   system is inspected and verified independently. A commercial revenue meter is set, sealed, and read by the
   utility, not by the customer. Elevators, boilers, fire-suppression systems, and structural welds in this state
   are all verified by a party other than the one whose work is being verified.

   The integrity principle is uniform across Texas utility regulation: the party consuming a shared public
   resource does not self-certify its own consumption. SB 6 itself embodies this - it routes large-load

   industrialized housing and buildings, a third-party inspection agency is an approved person or entity
   determined to be qualified by reason of facilities, personnel, experience, demonstrated reliability,

   compliance-control program, and the applicable code. The individual third-party inspector is defined in
