   IV.C The Deterministic Heat-and-Water Chain

   Data-center energy use is not an abstract metric. It is a physical event connected to local grid and water
   infrastructure through a deterministic three-link chain. Each link is an identity or a bounded engineering
   ratio, not an assumption, and each is derived with worked arithmetic in Annex I.

   IV.C. 1 Link one - electrical draw to heat
   Computational silicon performs no mechanical work and stores no significant energy. Essentially all
   electrical power delivered to it is converted to heat:

     Q [BTU/hr] = P [W] x 3.412142         equivalently     Q [BTU/hr] = P [MW] x 3,412,142


   This is a unit identity, not a model. A 150 kW rack rejects 511,821 BTU/hr - approximately 42.7 tons of
   refrigeration at the 12,000 BTU/hr refrigeration ton, or the continuous output of roughly five to six typical
   residential furnaces rated at 80,000-100,000 BTU/hr input.

   IV.C.2 Link two - heat to cooling energy
   Removing that thermal energy requires cooling power. In high-density operations, cooling and facility
   overhead account for approximately 30-40 percent of total facility electricity; air cooling demands roughly
   an additional 0.3-0.5 W of cooling power for every 1 W of active IT load. Expressed as power usage
   effectiveness:

     Plotal facility = PIT x PUE   where PUE = 1.15-1.25 (dry, mild) to 1.50-1.70+ (extreme ambient)


   The reported electrical figure must therefore be the gross facility figure. Reporting critical IT load alone
   understates the physical draw on the grid by the entire cooling and infrastructure fraction - which is to
   say, by exactly the fraction that grows during the summer hours when the grid is most constrained.

   IV.C.3 Link three - cooling to water consumption
   Where heat is rejected evaporatively, water is consumed by phase change. The consumed mass follows
   from the latent heat of vaporization:

     At hfg = 1,050 BTU/lb (typical of tower operating temperatures):
     1 MW of heat rejected evaporatively = 3,412,142 + 1,050 + 8.34 = 389.6 gal/hr = 9,352 gal/MW-day

   gal/hr per MW. The cooling-tower rule of thumb - evaporation of approximately one percent of

   fully evaporative facility is therefore approximately 390-410 gal/hr per MW of heat rejected, and this

   IV.D Axis 1 - Workload Profile Classification (Classes W-1, W-2, W-3)

   Axis 1 classifies a facility, or a circuit within a facility, by the shape of its electrical load over time. Shape is
   the property that determines how much capacity a utility must hold in reserve, and it is the property that a
   time-averaged reading destroys.

   Class W-1 - Continuous High-Utilization (AI Training / HPC)
   Class W-1 defines computational workloads characterized by a high, flat, and uninterrupted electrical load
   shape. It represents the most energy-dense and thermally intense operational class in modern data-center
   infrastructure.

   1. Electrical load shape and utilization. Class W-1 workloads operate at 95 percent or greater sustained
   utilization for long, continuous execution runs, frequently measured in days or weeks. Unlike variable cloud

   virtually identical throughout the job run.

   2. Hardware and power density. Class W-1 is typical of AI model-training superclusters - integrated 8-
   GPU nodes such as H100, H200, or B200 class systems - and of continuous high-performance computing.
   Rack power densities range from 40 to 80+ kW per rack, extending to 150+ kW per rack in next-generation
   architectures. An integrated 8-GPU server node alone draws 6.5 to 7.5 kW.

   3. Thermal and water footprint. Because computational silicon converts essentially all electrical input
   into heat, Class W-1 facilities produce continuous maximum heat rejection. Beyond the 25-30 kW per rack
   threshold, air cooling fails, making direct liquid cooling or cold plates physically mandatory. When paired
   with evaporative cooling towers, this continuous thermal output drives sustained, maximum municipal
   water consumption - on the order of 390 gal/hr per MW of rejected heat, continuously, for the duration of
   the run (Annex I).

   4. Measurement and regulatory rule. Because peak and average draw are nearly identical, Class W-1
   loads cannot be concealed behind time-averaging - but neither can they be understated by it. Class W-1
   circuits must be metered at the secondary distribution bus or PDU level (the M2 transport boundary) using
   revenue-grade current-transformer submeters compliant with ANSI C12.20 or IEC 62053-22, together with
   open server telemetry, so that continuous grid and thermal strain is accurately attributed to the circuits
   producing it.


     Why W-1 is the reference class for water. A continuous class has no diversity. There is no hour of
     the day in which a training cluster's heat rejection falls off, and therefore no hour in which its
     evaporative makeup demand falls off. Utility planning practice that assumes a load factor materially
     below unity is inapplicable to Class W-1, and a water study that applies one to a W-1 facility
     understates the demand by the inverse of the assumed factor.

    Class C-1 defines cooling architectures where computational heat is rejected entirely to the ambient air
   using dry coolers or air-cooled chillers, without an evaporative water loop in normal operation. It is the dry
   baseline of Axis 2.

     • Infrastructure        and    mechanics.       Standard     mechanical   refrigeration   or   dry-fluid   coolers   -
        CRAC/CRAH units, air-cooled chillers, and air-side economizers - transferring thermal energy directly
        from IT equipment to ambient air.

     • Water consumption profile. A facility operating strictly within Class C-1 consumes near-zero cooling
        water in day-to-day operation, because no water is evaporated to atmosphere.

     • Conditional exemption. A facility claims Class C-1 status only so long as it operates no evaporative
        circuit and no evaporative add-on.
     • Reclassification trigger. If an air-cooled facility installs or engages any evaporative-assist mechanism
        - condenser-coil misting, spray pre-cooling, or adiabatic wetted pads during extreme summer ambient
        peaks - it automatically reclassifies as Class C-4 (Hybrid / Evaporative-Assisted).

     • Submetering requirement. On entering Class C-4 for that circuit, the facility becomes subject to the
        mandatory secondary point-of-use water submeter under the Two-Meter Method (proposed subsection
        (f)).
   Density limits and electrical trade-offs. Conventional air cooling reaches its physical boundary at
   approximately 25-30 kW per rack; facilities housing AI training racks at 40-80+ kW per rack physically
   cannot operate under pure Class C-1 air cooling and are forced into liquid-cooled regimes. And while Class
   C-1 preserves municipal water, air-cooled chillers require higher electrical input per watt of IT load at high
   ambient temperature - typically 0.3 to 0.5 W of cooling power per 1 W of IT load - exchanging water
   consumption for higher peak electrical demand on the grid. Class C-1 is therefore not the costless
   option; it is the option that moves the burden from the water utility to the electric utility, and it
   must be reported as such.

   Class C-2 - Closed-Loop / Recirculating Non-Evaporative
   Class C-2 defines cooling architectures using a sealed recirculating loop to transfer heat away from
   computational hardware without evaporating water to atmosphere.

   1. Core mechanics - the sealed loop. Class C-2 systems use sealed internal fluid loops (treated water,
   glycol, or dielectric fluid) running through liquid-to-liquid heat exchangers, rear-door heat exchangers, or
   direct liquid cooling cold plates mounted to CPU/GPU dies. Because the internal loop is sealed, water
   recirculates continuously with zero operational evaporation or blowdown discharge from that loop.

   2. The outdoor rejection condition - closing the C-2 / C-3 loophole. A closed indoor liquid loop is
   not, on its own, sufficient to claim Class C-2 status. Class C-2 holds only if heat rejection to the outside is
   also non-evaporative - dry fluid coolers or air-cooled radiators. If a facility uses a closed indoor liquid loop
   but rejects that heat outdoors using evaporative cooling towers, adiabatic wetted media, or spray ponds,
   the facility is not Class C-2. It is Class C-3, because the consumptive water loss occurs at the outdoor
   heat-rejection stage.

   3. Texas summer heat and the Class C-4 transition. During extreme Texas ambient dry-bulb heat,
   outdoor dry coolers often cannot reject heat from high-density racks within design approach. If a Class C-2
   facility engages any evaporative assist - spray misting, condenser-coil pre-cooling, or wetted adiabatic
   pads - the facility automatically changes class to Class C-4 for that circuit, and that circuit becomes
   immediately subject to the secondary point-of-use submeter under 16 TAC § 24.283 and Tex. Water Code
   Ch. 13, Subch. M.

   training (40-80+ kW/rack) and next-generation (150+ kW/rack) pods that exceed the air-cooling limit.
   When paired with dry outdoor heat rejection, true Class C-2 facilities preserve municipal water resources
   but, like Class C-1, require higher outdoor fan and compressor energy during peak summer heat.

   Class C-3 - Evaporative / Cooling Towers / Adiabatic
   Class C-3 defines architectures where heat is rejected directly to atmosphere by evaporating water. It is
   the most water-consumptive cooling classification and the primary technical focus of the Two-Meter
   Method.

   1. Core mechanics and water loss. Class C-3 systems rely on open or closed-circuit cooling towers,
   evaporative condensers, wetted-media adiabatic systems, or spray ponds. Thermal energy is transferred to
   a water loop and rejected as water changes phase from liquid to vapor. Water loss is an unavoidable
   thermodynamic consequence of operation and consists of:

     • Evaporative loss - water converted to vapor and lost to atmosphere (-390 gal/hr per MW rejected);

     • Drift - entrained droplets carried out of the tower, bounded at roughly 0.005 percent of recirculating
        flow by drift eliminators, and consumptive;
     • Blowdown / bleed-off - concentrated water discharged to sewer to prevent scale, equal to
        evaporation divided by (COC - 1), and withdrawn but not consumed.

   2. The outdoor heat-rejection rule (distinguishing C-2 from C-3). A common misconception is that a
   facility with closed indoor liquid loops - direct-to-chip cold plates or rear-door heat exchangers - is
   automatically a closed-loop facility. The standard establishes the opposite: classification is governed by
   where the evaporative water loss physically occurs. A closed indoor loop rejecting heat outdoors
   through evaporative towers or wetted media is Class C-3.

   3. The mandatory Two-Meter Method.

     • Primary service-entrance meter - the standard utility master meter measuring total water intake
        delivered to the property line.
     • Secondary point-Of-use submeter - an ordinary, off-the-shelf water meter installed at the feed line
        entering the evaporative cooling tower or loop.
     • Calculating consumptive loss - metering the evaporative feed directly identifies the water entering the
        evaporative circuit; the portion of that feed that does not return as metered or conductivity-derived
        blowdown is the quantity consumed to atmosphere. This eliminates reliance on fictional drain-line
        estimates.

   4. Statutory grounding and municipal system protection. The secondary meter requires no
   specialized or proprietary hardware; it is the point-of-use submeter authorized under 16 TAC § 24.283 and
   Texas Water Code Ch. 13, Subch. M. Large continuous evaporative draws can depress local water system
   pressures; metering Class C-3 feeds ensures the draw can be evaluated against the 35 psi design and
   operating floors and the capacity requirements of 30 TAC §§ 290.44(d), 290.45, and 290.46(r).

   Class C-4 - Hybrid / Evaporative-Assisted
   Class C-4 defines air-cooled or closed-loop systems fitted with supplemental evaporative assist -
   condenser-coil misting, spray pre-cooling, or wetted adiabatic pads - that engage during high ambient
   temperature conditions. It is the mechanism that captures evaporative water consumption occurring during
   extreme summer heat waves, which is exactly when it is least visible and most damaging.

   IV.G Workload Separation: Uniformity as the Decisive Property

   The justification for moving the regulatory measurement boundary from the facility fence (Ml) to the



GRUS · Petition for Adoption ofa Rule · 16 TAC § 25.- PUC Project No. 60084                                            Page 17 of 33
    internal transport boundary (M2) is physical load uniformity.

   Uniform loads (steady state). General compute, database, storage, and transactional applications run at
   low, predictable, steady draws. Their flat thermal and electrical footprints integrate easily into standard
   utility forecasting, and an averaged reading describes them accurately.

   Non-uniform loads (volatile peaks). AI model training (95 percent or greater sustained utilization) and
   large-model inference (demand-driven fluctuation between 40 and 100 percent of TDP) create highly
   variable or continuously maximal draws whose peak is the planning-relevant quantity. For these, an
   averaged reading is not merely imprecise; it describes a facility that does not exist.

   The socialization gap. Standard fence meters average volatile, high-amplitude spikes over billing
   intervals. This hides the physical peaks that force the utility to build grid capacity, upgrade transmission
   transformers, and secure additional water capacity. The capacity is built and paid for regardless; the only
   question the averaging resolves is who pays. Where the causing load is invisible , the cost defaults to the
   general rate base.

   The resolution - M2 isolation. Transport-boundary meters resolve power draw per circuit at the
   internal power distribution unit level. As demonstrated by drawing GRUS-GRID-005 (Exhibit 4), on a single
   reference PDU panel, four non-uniform AI circuits of eight total circuits drive approximately 168 A of
   approximately 256 A of peak draw and approximately 115 kWth of approximately 142.5 kWth of heat - and
   therefore the corresponding majority of cooling-water consumption - while general compute, database,
   and storage circuits draw a small, steady, uniform fraction. The aggregate fence meter sees only the
   summed current and cannot resolve that four circuits are responsible. The M2 meter resolves it per circuit.

   Drawing GRUS-GRID-001 (Exhibit 1) establishes why this is not an arbitrary point of insertion: the same
   distribution hierarchy, the same step-down stages, and the same measurement-node structure recur at
   every scale from generation to the processor die. M2 is not a new kind of node invented for this rule;
   it is the same kind of node as Ml, placed one level in.

   What resolution does and does not conclude. The panel schedule resolves where physical strain concentrates. It does not
   conclude that any facility should be denied service, curlailed, or charged a particular rate. Those are determinations for the
   Commission and the affected utilities on a measured record. Pelilioner supplies the measurement; the State draws the
   conclusion.

   The three reported quantities at paragraph (3) are not redundant. Total intake is what the supplying
   utility must deliver, and is the figure relevant to source, treatment, and pumping capacity. Evaporative
   feed is what must be delivered at the moment of ambient peak, and is the figure relevant to distribution
   pressure. Consumptive loss is what never comes back, and is the figure relevant to basin, aquifer, and
   regional planning. Blowdown is the figure relevant to the wastewater plant, because it returns
   concentrated in dissolved solids. One number cannot serve four authorities; three metered quantities can
   serve all four.

   Answering the principal engineering objection. The principal objection to water measurement at
   computational facilities is that consumptive loss cannot be metered because evaporation leaves no stream
   to meter. The objection is correct about the vapor and irrelevant to the method. Evaporation is measured
   by difference at the feed, in the same way any consumptive process is measured: by metering what goes in
   and accounting for what comes back out. Cycles of concentration are determined by conductivity, an
   ordinary and continuously logged tower measurement, which is why the return fraction is a determinable
   quantity rather than an assumption. Paragraphs (2) and (6) state one method, not two: (2) gives the
   arithmetic and (6) states the physical point of measurement and forecloses the drain-line objection.

   necessary to evaluate compliance with 30 TAC § 290.44(d) (design: minimum 35 psi at all points at flow
   rates of at least 1.5 gpm per connection; 20 psi under combined fire and drinking-water flow), 30 TAC §
   290.46(r) (operation: minimum 35 psi under normal operating conditions; 20 psi during emergencies such
   as firefighting), and 30 TAC § 290.45 (minimum system capacity). Absent a secondary evaporative meter,
   compliance with those floors can only be asserted, and failure surfaces only when a smaller system is
   physically overtaxed. The design floor and the operating floor are separate obligations and fail in different
   ways: a system lawfully designed to 35 psi at 1.5 gpm per connection may still fall below 35 psi in operation
   once a continuous multi-hundred-gallon-per-hour evaporative draw is added at a single node during a

               PART VI - WHY THESE BELONG INSIDE THE MEASUREMENT

   6.1 Each subsection specifies the measurement itself
   Each proposed subsection specifies a necessary element of the measurement: what it measures on the
   water leg (subsection (f), the secondary evaporative meter and the Two-Meter Method) and on the
   electrical leg (subsection (i), the two-tier bus submeter and existing telemetry); who verifies it (subsection
   (g), a qualified party independent of the one being measured); the class it reads (subsections (d), (e), and
   (h), the two-axis profile); what its reading resolves (subsection (j), the jurisdiction); the evidentiary grade
   and scope of what is reported (subsection (k)); and the allocation the reading supports (subsection (1)).

   Remove any one and the standard cannot be applied uniformly. Without a boundary, two verifiers measure
   different things. Without a verifier standard, the boundary is read by an interested party. Without
   classification, the same reading means different things at different facilities. Without a common record,
   four authorities receive four partial answers. Without evidence grades, a projection and a measurement
   appear identical on the page. Without allocation, a correct measurement produces no consequence. These
   are the definitions the framework already requires in order to function, each grounded in a standard or
   statute already in force.

   6.2 The burden is minimal and the method is ordinary
   On the water leg: one commonplace point-of-use water meter at a defined point, added to a facility that
   already has a primary meter and is already required by SB 6 to submit water studies and to bear


GRUS · Petition for Adoption ofa Rule · 16 TAC § 25.- PUC Project No. 60084                                 Page 30 of 33
    interconnection costs. On the electrical leg: revenue-grade submeters of the type already installed for
   tenant allocation, plus a software configuration exposing telemetry the servers already produce. No novel
   instrument, no proprietary device, no tear-out, and no inspection of anything a facility has a legitimate
   interest in protecting.

   What it produces is the one quantity presently missing and unverifiable: how much water and how much
   peak power a large load actually consumes, measured at the point it occurs, verified by a party competent
   and independent enough to measure it, assessed against the correct facility class.

   6.3 What the whole converts
   Taken together, these subsections convert the mandated audit from a self-report the facility fills out - the
   method that already failed at better than ninety percent - into a measurement the State can stand behind:
   measured at a defined boundary by an ordinary secondary meter and standard bus submeters, verified by a
   qualified independent party, assessed against a stated facility class, and recorded in a form every affected
   authority can read.

   That is the entire proposal. It does not decide whether any facility should be built, connected, curtailed, or
   charged. It decides only that the quantities on which those decisions rest will be measured rather than
   asserted.

C.6 Core Forensic Rules for Heat-Transfer Boundary Audits
1. Governance by Q = UA ATim· Increasing heat-exchanger surface area (A) reduces the approach temperature, but
   cannot alter or lower the ambient dry-bulb or wet-bulb floor. No quantity of equipment moves the ambient condition.
2. Rejection of fictional continuous limits. An absolute equipment limit of 125 °F or 135 °F cannot be treated as a
   recommended continuous operating temperature when the manufacturer specifies 108 °F. A filing that operates the
   design case at the absolute rating is deficient under § V.F.1.
3. Misting reduction verification. Misting or adiabatic pre-cooling cannot be claimed to produce a fixed 20 °F or 23 °F
   temperature drop without documented dry-bulb, wet-bulb, and relative-humidity test logs. The claimed drop shall be
  stated as a saturation effectiveness against the measured wet-bulb, and effectiveness above 0.90 shall be supported by
  manufacturer test data at the stated ambient condition.
1. The wet-bulb floor is absolute. Evaporative cooling of any kind - tower, adiabatic pad, or fogging skid - cannot
   produce an air or water temperature below the ambient wet-bulb. Any filing whose design case implies otherwise is
  deficient on its face.
5. Water follows heat, not nameplate. Consumptive water is a function of heat actually rejected evaporatively, not of
   installed capacity. A facility operating at 60 percent load evaporates approximately 60 percent of the design rate; a
   facility at continuous 95 percent utilization (Class W-1) does not.

B.2 Thermodynamic Heat and Water Performance Analysis

B.2.1 The 25-30 kW per Rack Limit and the Air-Cooling Threshold
Physical threshold. Air cooling (Class C-1) reaches a hard thermodynamic and airflow limit near 25-30 kW per rack.
Above this density, liquid cooling - cold plates or direct-to-chip, Class C-2 - becomes a physical necessity rather than a
design preference.
The 108 °F OEM limit. While equipment may carry an absolute maximum rating of 125-135 °F, major dry-cooler
manufacturers specify approximately 108 °F dry-bulb as the maximum recommended continuous operating temperature.
Above it, fan power rises sharply and heat-exchanger approach temperatures break down. Annex B shows why this matters
in Texas specifically: at 108 °F and 30 percent relative humidity, 28.0 °F of evaporative potential remains available, and a
facility can hold full load by engaging an assist - which is precisely the moment it becomes a Class C-4 facility and incurs
the obligation of § V.A.

B.2.2 Evaporative Water Consumption Dynamics
Latent heat conversion. Rejecting 1 MW of heat evaporatively requires 3,412,142 BTU/hr of latent capacity. At hfg -
1,050 BTU/lb this consumes approximately 390 gal/hr per MW - approximately 9,350 gallons per MW-day of pure
evaporation, before blowdown. Including blowdown at typical cycles of concentration, total makeup runs approximately
10,700-14,000 gallons per MW-day (Part IV.C.3).
A single 150 kW AI rack. Rejects 511,821 BTU/hr - approximately 42.7 tons of refrigeration, or the continuous output of
roughly five to six residential furnaces. Under full evaporative rejection it evaporates approximately 1,400 gallons per day
and requires approximately 1,700-2,100 gallons per day of makeup depending on cycles of concentration - comparable to
the daily water demand of roughly eight to ten suburban households, from a single rack.

B.2.3 The Multi-Day Sustained Heat-Wave Risk
Coincident infrastructure stress. Continuous 108 °F-plus heat waves force Class C-3 and Class C-4 systems to operate at
or near full evaporative capacity for 72 or more consecutive hours. Unlike a single-day peak, a multi-day event gives
municipal storage no overnight recovery window, because the facility's draw does not fall at night and residential irrigation
demand resumes each morning against depleted elevated storage.
Municipal main depletion. These high-volume, uninterrupted draws depress municipal distribution mains, risking failure

ambient conditions at which this transition predictably occurs, which is why the transition can be audited rather than

D.1 Key Operational Findings
1. The Class C-4 transition trigger. In the hot/dry case, dry coolers reach their sensible rejection threshold. Engaging
   spray misting or adiabatic media depresses entering air toward the wet-bulb, maintaining 100 percent IT load capacity
   - and automatically reclassifying the circuit to Class C-4, triggering mandatory point-of-use submetering under 16 TAC
   § 24.283. The facility keeps its load by spending municipal water, and the standard's only requirement is that
  the spending be measured.
2. Wet-bulb compression in humid conditions. In the hot/humid case, high relative humidity compresses the
   evaporative potential to as little as 2.5-9 °F. Evaporative efficiency collapses precisely when heat rejection is hardest,
   forcing centrifugal chillers to carry the load and driving cooling overhead to +0.55 W per 1 W of IT. Water use does not
  fall in this case; blowdown rises as cycles concentrate, and the electrical draw rises alongside it.
3. Multi-day extreme strain. During sustained 108 °F-plus conditions, high-density AI clusters consume up to roughly
   2,100 gallons per day per 150 kW rack of makeup water while simultaneously imposing their maximum electrical
   demand. The two peaks are coincident by construction, not by coincidence - both are driven by the same ambient
  condition on the same afternoon as peak residential demand.
1. There is no water-free option at extreme ambient. A facility that avoids evaporative water entirely pays for it in
   electrical overhead at PUE 1.5-1.7 during precisely the hours ERCOT is most constrained. The two axes trade against
  each other, and a measurement standard that reads only one of them can be satisfied by moving the burden to the other.

E.4.2 The six-tier relationship classification
The relationship between a facility's water draw and a system event must be classified under one of six defined categories,
and never by timing alone:
1. No demonstrated correlation - physical, hydraulic, or temporal evidence disproves any connection.

E.4.3 Hydraulic mechanisms
Scouring velocities and hydraulic transients. Rapid, un-ramped valve openings for cooling-tower makeup or high-
pressure adiabatic spray (Classes C-3 and C-4) cause sudden velocity spikes in distribution mains. High velocity scours iron
and manganese tuberculation from older pipe walls, discoloring water throughout the pressure zone.
Pressure floor breaches. Sustained evaporative makeup draws during peak summer can pull distribution pressure below
the 35 psi operating floor. Below 20 psi, back-siphonage risk rises and the applicable public-notification obligations attach.

 Why this protocol protects both directions. A rigorous incident protocol is as valuable to a well-run facility as to a
 municipality. Without submeter logs and a stated classification method, a facility located near an aging main will be
 blamed for every discolored-water call in its pressure zone, and will have no evidence with which to answer. With them,
 the six-tier classification distinguishes ordinary pipe aging from facility-induced strain on the record. Measurement is
 the only thing that makes exoneration possible.

F. 5 Statutory Takeaways
1. Water submetering is already codified. The Two-Meter Method requires no new statutory authority. Texas already
   recognizes point-of-use submeters under 16 TAC § 24.283 and Texas Water Code Ch. 13, Subch. M. Applying that

2. Independent verification is already defined. Rather than creating new administrative definitions, the rule adopts the
   independence-of-judgment standard at 16 TAC § 70.10(a) and the attestation criteria at § 70.23(b)(4). That supplies a
   legal mechanism to execute the Governor's audit directive and to cure the documented failure of self-reporting.
3. One statute drives both boundaries. PURA § 35.004(c-1) requires large loads to contribute to interconnection and
   infrastructure cost recovery. Measuring electrical draw at the M2 transport boundary with revenue-grade instruments
   supplies the resolution necessary to assign caused cost to the causing load, and to insulate residential and small-

 ANNEX G - REGIONAL AGGREGATION AND CUMULATIVE STRAIN
Computational load and infrastructure audits must never be conducted in isolation. Evaluating a single facility alone
creates a false sense of security: a project requesting 50 MW of power or 0.5 MGD of water may appear manageable on its

pressure zones.

   THE INDISCRIMINATE READING - A FEW WORKLOAD CLASSES DRIVE MOST OF THE STRAIN
   Across the full landscape, the meter reads every class the same way. The result is not uniform: circuits 1-17 (AI training + large-model inference) carry the great
   majority of peak draw (-168 of -256 A) and heat (-115 of -142.5 kW), and therefore the great majority of cooling-waterconsumption - while general compute,
   database, and storage (circuits 23-33) are a small, steady, uniform fraction. On one panel, four circuits produce most of the physical strain on grid and water.

   The aggregate fence meter sees only the -256 A sum and cannot resolve that four circuits are responsible. The transport-boundary meter (M2) resolves it per
   circuit. That resolution - indiscriminate across all classes, revealing where strain concentrates - is the entire purpose of the meter. GRUS draws no conclusion; the State does.




 GENERAL NOTES & SOURCING
 1. All draw/density figures are published. vendor-neutral industr·y values (device TDP: CPU 150250W. Hl-class GPU --700W, 8-GPU server 5.6-7.5kW;
 rack density: traditional 5-15kW, AI training 40-80kW, next-gen 150kW+). No proprietary oroperator-specific data is used.
 2. Heat = electrical power consumed (BTU/hr == W x 3.412). Cooling == 30-40% of facility electricity: -0.3-0.5W cooling per 1W IT. Water scales with heat rejected.
 3. Uniformity is the decisive property: non-uniform loads (AI training/inference) have bursty peaks the aggregate meter averages away; only fine-resolution
 metering at the transport boundary resolves them. This is the physical justification for M2.

 4. This schedule characterizes workload CLASSES by published draw. It identifies no operator and targets no party. Internal mechanism (CMM/Il-Il) held.
 5. NOTE: Reference figures for characterization. Facility-specific values sealed by a licensed PE. Peak draw per NEC sized at 125% of continuous load.
